item.title: A Tale of Two Chinas
item.description: China’s economy is deeply unbalanced, with a battered real-estate sector, weak consumption, and stark regional disparities coexisting with dynamic tech and export sectors. But provided that political stability is maintained, China could continue to be a global powerhouse even as hundreds of millions of its citizens remain poor.

item.title: Sino–American Stability?
item.description: Delegates at the Bund Summit in Shanghai largely agreed that the US-China relationship could be entering a new, less contentious chapter, although many were more interested in what the post-Trump era will mean for Sino-American ties. But perhaps the most heartening sign for the future was the honest exchange of views.

item.title: Europe’s Winter of Discontent
item.description: Although it is true that European integration has always been forged through crisis, the continent’s postwar story was largely one of incremental responses to relatively manageable challenges. Today, the European Union is facing multiple, interrelated problems that challenge its very raison d’être.

item.title: How Students Dethroned Serbia’s Strongman
item.description: Following the ouster of Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán after 16 years in power earlier this year, the world has once again witnessed the merits of “old-school” campaigning. In toppling their own country's strongman, Serbia's new student-led opposition offers important lessons for those defending democracy elsewhere.

item.title: What a US-China AI Safety Channel Needs
item.description: Addressing AI safety risks depends on close collaboration between the two leading AI powers, and the establishment of an incident-reporting channel is just a small step in this direction. But success will require that the US and Chinese governments actually understand what is happening under their own noses.

item.title: The Authoritarian Logic of Selective Privacy
item.description: Around the world, governments are increasingly deciding who gets privacy and who is denied it, a double standard that turns a fundamental democratic right into a privilege. US President Donald Trump’s administration is a prime example, shielding ICE agents from scrutiny while expanding surveillance of immigrants and protesters.

item.title: Brazil’s Chapter in the Anti-Authoritarian Playbook
item.description: Brazil’s renewed democratic confidence must now be matched by institutional and structural reforms and a willingness to build coalitions beyond the left. Recent democratic outcomes in Hungary and Serbia offer useful lessons.

item.title: Another Crash Landing for Brazil’s Economy?
item.description: Brazil’s floating exchange rate, high foreign-exchange reserves, strong commodity exports, and debt denominated predominantly in its own currency reduce its exposure to a balance-of-payments crisis. Nonetheless, continued fiscal deterioration under President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will carry high domestic costs.

item.title: Europe’s Make-or-Break Moment Has Arrived
item.description: US President Donald Trump has not only abandoned Ukraine and America’s European allies, but has increasingly sided with Russian President Vladimir Putin. To preserve their sovereignty, Europeans must remain united in the face of outside pressure, which in turn requires managing political threats from within their borders.

item.title: Middle Powers Can Lead on AI Safety
item.description: With the United States showing no interest in regulating AI, middle powers have an opportunity to take the lead on governance. By banding together, these countries could condition market access on meeting a common set of safety requirements and explore joint investment in technical capacity.

item.title: Lula Killed the Donroe Doctrine
item.description: In attempting to disentangle the United States from the rest of the world and retreat into a seemingly controllable hemispheric stronghold, Donald Trump's Latin America strategy had fared better than the rest of his foreign policy. But following a defeat for the far right in Brazil, his project now looks dead in the water.

item.title: The Wrong Way to Compare Economic Size
item.description: At the European Central Bank’s annual research conference, Paul Krugman concluded that, when it comes to “weaponized interdependence,” the EU is more powerful than both the US and China. But his reliance on PPP-adjusted GDP as a way to smooth out the volatility of nominal exchange rates ignores the even greater swings in PPP data.

item.title: Public Control for a Purposeful Economy
item.description: As more governments recognize the need for greater public control over economic outcomes, they must be careful to define the concept well. What ultimately matters is not ownership, but the state’s capacity to steer economic activity toward strategic objectives in the service of the common good.

item.title: Rethinking Sustainable Livelihoods From the Ground Up
item.description: In regions where economic activity has long revolved around fossil-fuel extraction, ensuring a just transition requires developing alternative livelihoods that account for each community’s specific needs. Regional endowment funds could be a useful vehicle for funding these local initiatives.

item.title: The Specter of an AI-Driven Slowdown
item.description: The rush to finance AI infrastructure is driving up borrowing costs just as governments grapple with mounting debt and persistent fiscal deficits. If the AI investment boom falters, falling valuations could choke off financing, with little room for fiscal and monetary policy to cushion the economic shock.

item.title: Is a Chinese Implosion Looming?
item.description: If current trends continue, the Chinese state will find itself exposed to a political succession crisis, a weakening economy, and a lack of resources to exercise power domestically and project it externally. It would be a perfect storm, with far-reaching global repercussions.

item.title: PS Events: Reinventing Europe – Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala
item.description: When we talk about "reinvention" we often overlook what works, noted WTO Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala in her closing keynote. This is true of the global trading system, which has proven surprisingly resilient in recent years, and of the European economy, which might not have a tech giant to rival those in the US or China, but remains a global trade powerhouse and a leader in science and research. While Europe has much to do to improve its external competitiveness, it must not act from a sense of panic. Instead, it must pursue measured reforms and seize new opportunities, not least closer trade and investment ties with Africa.

item.title: Who Pays the Fiscal Watchdogs?
item.description: Civil-society oversight is the cheapest insurance in sovereign finance, because it enables independent scrutiny long before a default. But given that a borrowing government will never volunteer to fund the people who audit it, global decision-makers must do so using agreements for stolen-asset recovery and sovereign-debt treatments.

item.title: How to Help Left-Behind Regions
item.description: Pouring public investment into poorer towns and cities might be politically beneficial, but the economic returns of indiscriminate largesse would be limited. A better approach would concentrate investment in areas with the potential to become high-productivity hubs, such as large peripheral cities.

item.title: The Agentic Information Economy
item.description: An internet populated and run by AI agents will need not just reliable data but also a broader information ecology capable of questioning its own inputs and transmitting corrections where they are needed if information changes. But whether this will serve private interests or the public good remains to be seen.
